query: Consider the following context: During the hot dip aluminum plating process, components such as sinking rollers, pulling rollers, and guide plates will come into long-term contact with high-temperature liquid aluminum and be corroded by the aluminum liquid, greatly reducing their service life. In that context, which material can be used for prepare parts for the dipping and plating equipment and protect the equipment from erosion, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A refractory high‐entropy alloy (RHEA) with an optimized composition that includes a relatively high aluminum content can, upon exposure to liquid aluminum at high temperatures, rapidly form a dense, self‐healing alumina (Al2O3) surface layer that reduces erosion of dipping equipment components during hot dip aluminum plating.
generation.material_initial_state: A standard metal alloy currently used in dipping equipment, which does not intentionally form a protective oxide film under high‐temperature conditions.
generation.intervention: Replace the conventional alloy with a RHEA engineered (for example, a modified AlNbTaTiVZr system) to promote alumina formation.
generation.conditions: Simulated hot dip aluminum plating conditions that involve prolonged high-temperature immersion in liquid aluminum along with mechanical contacts similar to those experienced by sinking rollers, pulling rollers, and guide plates.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a dense and adherent Al2O3 scale on the surface of the RHEA.
generation.mechanism: The enhanced aluminum content and the multi-element design encourage diffusion of Al to the surface. At the high plating temperatures, this leads to the in situ development of a compact, self-healing alumina layer that acts as a barrier to further chemical attack and metal dissolution.
generation.predicted_outcome: Components made from the optimized RHEA will exhibit significantly lower mass loss and surface degradation compared with the conventional alloys, resulting in improved resistance to erosion under hot dip aluminum plating conditions.
generation.baseline: Performance metrics of existing dipping equipment components made from conventional alloys under the same hot dip plating conditions.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of the protective alumina layer may depend on the stability of the oxide under continuous mechanical stress and thermal cycling. Furthermore, the precise durability under extreme conditions of wear remains to be validated.
generation.uncertainty: Although prior studies suggest that an optimized alloy composition can promote protective oxide formation, the long-term behavior of such a RHEA in dynamic liquid aluminum exposure and under mechanical contact has not been fully characterized.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of dipping equipment components: one set made from the optimized RHEA and a control set made from the conventional alloy. Subject both sets to a laboratory simulation of hot dip aluminum plating conditions, including prolonged high-temperature immersion in liquid aluminum and cyclical mechanical loading. Periodically remove samples for surface analysis.
measurements: Surface morphology and oxide layer thickness using SEM/EDS
Mechanical integrity testing (e.g., hardness, adhesion of oxide layer)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the RHEA components do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in mass loss and surface degradation, or if a stable and dense alumina layer is not evidenced by surface characterization compared to the conventional alloy, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) first appeared in public view in 2010 [ [1] ]. Thereafter, they aroused great concern from researchers at home and abroad. Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [ [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. RHEAs, with excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures, are considered promising high-temperature application materials, which are suitable for complex working conditions such as atomic energy, aerospace, the military industry, advanced nuclear reactors, etc. Previous studies focused on mechanical properties at high- and room-temperatures, but with little research and analysis on high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [7] , [8] , [9] ]. The research shows that adding the proper amount of Al, Cr, and Si elements into the refractory high-entropy alloy can form a dense oxidation film on the surface of the alloy in a high-temperature environment, thus improving the high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [10] , [11] , [12] , [13] ]. The Al 0.5 NbTa 0.8 Ti 1.5 V 0.2 Zr alloy was prepared by vacuum/argon arc melting using high purity (99.9% or higher) elements. Details of the alloy preparation are given elsewhere [9] . After solidification on a water-cooled copper hearth, the alloy was hot iso-statically pressed (HIP’d) at 1200 °C for 2 hours under a super-high purity argon pressure of 210 MPa. After that it was homogenized by holding at 1200 °C for 24 h in a tube furnace with a continuous flow of high purity argon and then slow cooled at 10 °C/min. This condition is called Condition (1). A piece of the sample in Condition (1) was sealed in a quartz tube filled with high purity argon and additionally annealed at 1400 °C for 20 min and water quenched. This condition is called Condition (2). Corrosion resistance of alloys in light water reactors (LWRs) and more generally in oxidative environments is achieved by the formation of protective oxide layers that hinder further oxidation. Alloys containing Cr, Al, or Si typically tend to form a compact and self-healing chromia (Cr 2 O 3 ), alumina (Al 2 O 3 ) or silica (SiO 2 ) layers, respectively, which acts as effective diffusion barriers against further oxidation [1] – [3] . However, in molten fluoride salts (salt of choice for many molten salt reactor concepts, MSRs) these protective oxide layers on structural alloys are unstable which in turn leads to the dissolution of the least noble element in the alloy. Such a corrosion mechanism can lead to a reduction in components’ wall thickness and eventually the loss of the structural integrity of the reactor components [1] , [2] . The dissolution products themselves may lead to plate-out in the relatively cooler sections of the system due to the strong sensitivity of solubility of analytes to temperature.

chosen.why: The open question precisely asks which material can be used for protective parts—and why—under high-temperature aluminum corrosion. Prior studies often covered limited material systems or used oversimplified test conditions. By systematically varying the material composition and using standard corrosion and surface characterization techniques under realistic plating conditions, the study directly fills the identified gap. This approach leverages a well-established experimental framework in materials science to address the erosion mechanism and identify a high-performance protective material suitable for the process.
